extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne / students of philosophical essays and personal reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive maxims for living, judging, and learning as expressed in Montaigne's essay 'Of Experience' — useful for readers and writers of reflective personal essays and those studying practical philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of experience as a means to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience is a means to knowledge that, though weaker and cheaper than reason, should not be disdained; truth is great and all mediations that lead to it are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts experience with reason: both have many forms and both can mislead, but because truth is important one should accept any mediation (including experience) that might guide to it. Example: learning from one’s own past mistakes is more practically instructive than merely abstract reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and respect diversity and dissimilarity
rubrics_metrics.description: No art or law can reach perfect similitude; nature and human affairs are marked by infinite variety, so universal prescriptions will always fall short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because events and individuals differ, rules and comparisons are always imperfect. Use general rules sparingly and be alert to particular differences; do not assume one example maps exactly to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and generality of laws over multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive multiplication of laws and minute divisions increases license and dispute rather than diminishing it; better a few simple, general laws than a prodigious number of particular ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that detailed statutory catalogues cannot cover infinite human actions and that too many laws leave wide room for divergent interpretation. Policy implication: prefer rare, simple, general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation breeds further dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: There is as much liberty in interpreting laws as in making them; commentaries and glosses multiply doubts rather than clear them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more commentators and interpretations accumulate, the more obscure and contested a text becomes. Anti-pattern: piling on successive glosses expecting to reach final clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of learned subtilty; avoid over-refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive scholastic refinement and subdivision (of language, doctrines, or law) irritate natural liberty and produce confusion and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: pressing quicksilver — the harder you subdivide, the more it disperses. Practical advice: avoid contriving artificial sentences/terms that obscure plain meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer nature’s simple prudence to artificial invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural prudence — a quiet, easy, salutary sense applied sincerely — often performs better in life than the pompous, intricate prudence invented by philosophers or lawyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses trusting simple, practical judgement given by nature rather than elaborate theoretical schemes; implication for conduct and writing: favor plain practical judgment over ornate theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know thyself as the cornerstone of prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: The injunction to 'know oneself' is of primary importance; self-knowledge (examining one’s own passions, errors, and limits) is the basis of prudence and the reform of one’s judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne presents self-examination as the practical path to wisdom: recalling past mistakes tempers future arrogance and helps to anticipate passions. He cites Plato and Socrates to support the centrality of self-knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal experience as primary moral and practical example
rubrics_metrics.description: A man’s own life and experiences often provide better instruction for conduct than canonical lives (e.g., Caesar) or abstract models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne claims the life of Caesar is no greater a guide than our own lived experience; writers and learners should prioritize concrete personal lessons over distant exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be modest and suspect certainty; avoid obstinate affirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmation and obstinacy are signs of lack of wit; one should hold opinions with modesty and be ready to suspect one’s own understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises modesty born of recognizing one’s repeated errors. Anti-pattern: dogmatic assertion without perception or experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning can increase difficulty and doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal learning and commentary often beget complexity and difficulty ('Difficultatem facit doctrina'); education can expand the field of doubts rather than resolve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware the tendency of scholarship to multiply problems; a generous mind will continue to inquire, but scholarship without application may only produce perplexity and 'puzzling' speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment should resist corruption by appetites and passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment should keep a 'magisterial seat' apart from appetites, hatred, and friendship; even if it cannot reform other parts, it must not be corrupted by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne emphasizes separating evaluative reason from personal biases and emotions. Practical advice: cultivate impartial judgment even amid strong personal inclinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal forms and procedures can produce injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect for judicial forms and technicalities can lead to grave injustice (e.g., executing innocent people because reversal would disturb forms), so the forms of justice can harm the substance of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: judges kept to form and sacrificed innocents; Philip compensated after recognizing a mistaken fine. Implication: procedures should not be elevated above substantive fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lawsuits and legal entanglements where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: One should abhor lawsuits and legal contests because they often do more harm than good, exposing people to risk and injustice and curtailing liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne relates community fear of being near a murder to avoid legal suspicion; practical norm: prefer retreat from rights when litigation would cost more than the right’s exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use errors and memory-failures as lessons to distrust one’s testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing the many errors of one’s own memory and judgment is more valuable than learning isolated facts — it teaches one to suspect one’s testimony and to rely less blindly on oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne treats his recollected false steps as reforms to overall conduct: upon encountering contrary reason, learn the general lesson of intellectual frailty rather than merely adopt the specific new fact.
